title: The BFF Pattern
description: Learn why backends-for-frontends emerged as a critical pattern for serving mobile, web, and IoT clients with tailored payloads, and how Netflix and Shopify evolved their gateway architectures.

segments.text: Here's a real problem that hits every company at scale. Your mobile app needs a compact payload — maybe two kilobytes. Your web dashboard needs rich data — fifty kilobytes. One API serving both means someone always loses.

This is the over-fetching problem. Mobile gets forty-eight kilobytes it doesn't need, burning battery and data plans. Netflix found their Android app was downloading three times more data than necessary because APIs were designed for the TV interface first.

The Backend-for-Frontend pattern solves this. Each client type gets its own dedicated backend service. Mobile BFF, web BFF, TV BFF. Each one aggregates exactly the data its client needs — no more, no less.

The BFF acts as an aggregation layer. A single mobile screen might need data from five microservices — user profile, notifications, feed, recommendations, and settings. The BFF makes those five calls, merges results, and returns one optimized response.
But wait. If each client type has its own BFF, and you have five client types, that's five services to maintain. Think about what could go wrong with this approach.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the risk of having separate BFF services for each client type?

segments.text: Code duplication. The Shopify team discovered their mobile and web BFFs had seventy percent overlapping logic. Business rule changes required updates in multiple places. They evolved toward a shared BFF with client-specific resolvers, keeping the benefits without the duplication tax.

Netflix took a different path — GraphQL federation. Instead of separate BFFs, they built a single federated graph. Each microservice owns its part of the schema. Clients query exactly the fields they need. The mobile app requests five fields, the TV app requests twenty, same endpoint.

Netflix's federated gateway handles over two billion GraphQL queries per day. Their supergraph stitches together schemas from hundreds of microservices. Each team owns their subgraph independently, deploying without coordination. That's the key — organizational scalability, not just technical.

Here's the tradeoff matrix. REST BFF: simple, full control per client, but duplication risk. GraphQL BFF: flexible queries, no over-fetching, but query complexity attacks and N-plus-one database problems if you're not careful with DataLoader batching.
In a Staff-level interview, you'll be asked which approach to choose. The answer depends on team structure. Conway's Law applies here directly.
segments.thought_prompt: If you have three client teams and twenty backend teams, which BFF approach would you choose and why?

segments.text: Production lessons learned: always set timeout budgets per downstream call in your BFF. If the recommendations service is slow, return the page without recommendations — don't block the entire response. Shopify uses a fifty-millisecond timeout per service with graceful degradation. Users get a partial page, not an error page.

The BFF pattern is really about matching your API layer to your organizational and client reality. Start with one BFF per distinct client experience, use GraphQL federation when your service count exceeds what manual aggregation can handle, and always design for partial failure. Next, we'll see how service meshes handle the communication layer beneath your BFFs.
